Eyan.note: A multilingual god list aligns Kothar with the Hurrian Eyan.

Ešem-Bethel.note: Anat-Bethel and Ešem-Bethel receive allocations in the same cultic account.

Gapnu.note: Baal sends Gapnu as one of his paired messengers to Mot.

Gaṯaru.note: Yarikh may occur with Gaṯaru in plural or dual ritual groupings.

Ge.note: Ge is the mother of Elus or Kronos in Philo’s genealogy.

Gupan.note: Baal dispatches Gupan as a divine messenger during palace negotiations and communications with Mot.
Gupan carries Baal’s message to Kothar at his distant residence.

Gupan and Ugar.note: The divine messengers convey Baal's speeches while avoiding Mot's devouring mouth.
Baal directs his two messengers to accompany Šapšu along her underworld route.

Habayu.note: Modern scholarship proposes Habayu as a name or form of Resheph.

Haddu/Hadad.note: Ugaritic poetry treats Haddu or Hadad as the same storm-god as Baal.

Harmakhis.note: Hauron fuses with Harmakhis, and both names designate the Great Sphinx.

Hulelu.note: They are his daughters if the disputed phrase bnt hll names a deity.

Hygieia.note: Hygieia is paired with Asklepios in a later Kition cult possibly continuing Eshmun's sanctuary.

Hypsouranios.note: Philo places Chousor among the descendants of Hypsouranios.

Hêlēl.myth: Fall of the shining son of Dawn
Hêlēl.note: Isaiah poetically styles the fallen celestial figure as Dawn's son.

Ilat.note: Ilat appears with Baal among gods who feast or deliberate.

Iolaus.myth: Iolaus revives Heracles with a quail
Iolaus.note: Iolaus restores the dead Tyrian Heracles using a quail beneath his nose.

Iolaus.myth: Hannibal and Philip's divine treaty witnesses
Iolaus.note: Heracles and Iolaus jointly appear among the gods guaranteeing the Carthaginian treaty.

Ishat.note: Anat includes the destructive female being Ishat among her defeated enemies.

IŠTAR-logogram goddess.note: The goddess overhears Elkunirša’s plot and secretly warns its intended target.

Juno Caelestis.note: She appears beside African Saturn in the Roman transformation of the Tanit–Baal Hammon pair.

Kasʾa.note: The obscure lunar-phase deity appears with Yarikh; their precise relationship is unknown.

Kirta.note: Kirta is promised a place among the Rephaim and Ditanu’s assembly.

Kronos.note: Astarte rules with other gods under Kronos’s consent.
Adodos and Astarte reign under Kronos's consent in Philo's learned system.
Greek authors identify the Carthaginian recipient of child sacrifice as Kronos.
Philo explicitly equates the Phoenician Elus with Greek Kronos.

Kubaba.note: Resheph and Kubaba occur jointly, but damage obscures their relationship.

Kulitta.note: Kulitta occurs after Nikkal in a ritual offering sequence associated with Šauška.

Kumarbi.note: Learned comparison associates both senior gods as fathers of storm gods; direct cultic identity is uncertain.

Kušuḫ.note: Nikkal is paired with the Hurrian moon god as his spouse in ritual traditions.
Kušuḫ and Yarikh receive coordinated offerings while remaining distinct gods.
Their lunar functions and association with Nikkal suggest partial equivalence, not identity.

Kāmaṯu.note: Kāmaṯu and the pair are co-invoked without a narrated interaction.

Malik.note: Modern scholarship disputes whether Malik-like deities are cognates of biblical Molech.

Metharme.note: Adonis is an ordinary son of Metharme in the Cypriot genealogy.

Milku.note: Milku is named among the divine recipients in Horon’s anti-venom sequence.
Scholars connect the Rephaim’s representative Rapiu with Milku; no narrative meeting survives.
Milku and the pair are co-invoked without a narrated interaction.

Moirai.note: The Fates are reproached or petitioned over Adonis’s death.

Molech.note: Later interpreters conjecturally equate Chemosh with Molech through alleged sacrificial similarities.

Mother of the Stallion/Mare.note: The petitioner addresses Šapšu as mother and requests divine aid against venom.

Myrrha.note: Myrrha bears Adonis from within the tree into which she was transformed.

Nahar.note: Nahar appears beside Lotan and related sea-dragon adversaries; no separate encounter survives.
Poetic parallelism treats Yam and Nahar as one opponent, though earlier independence is possible.

Nanaya.note: Resheph and Nanaya appear together with Ḥirta in Palmyrene dedications.

Ninatta.note: Ninatta occurs after Nikkal in a ritual offering sequence associated with Šauška.

Niqmaddu.myth: The descent of the royal dead
Niqmaddu.note: The deceased king Niqmaddu is summoned alongside the ancient Rephaim during succession rites.

Nutrix Saturni.note: Scholars propose Tanit’s maternal aspect as an antecedent, but the identity is insecure.

Og.note: Og is characterized as the sole surviving remnant of the Rephaim.

Oulomos.note: Chousoros emerges as the offspring or emanation of Oulomos’s self-union.

Ouranos.note: Philo’s learned Phoenician-Greek genealogy makes Astarte a daughter of Ouranos.
Philo's Demarous is biologically Ouranos's son through a concubine given to Dagon.
Philo makes Zeus Demarous, a Hadad-linked figure, actually the son of Ouranos.
Elus or Kronos is the son of Ouranos in Philo’s genealogy.
Elus or Kronos rebels against, ambushes, and castrates Ouranos.

Peor.note: Milton makes Chemos a fallen angel and identifies him with Peor.

Phoenix.note: A lost Hesiodic tradition names Phoenix as Adonis’s father.

Pidray.note: Pidray is named as one of Baal's three daughters.
Pidray appears among the female members of Baal's household.
She is proposed as an alternative bride in the composition invoking the Kotharat.
Pidray is apparently offered to Yarikh instead of Nikkal, but Yarikh refuses her.
Pidray is proposed as an alternative bride, but Yarikh refuses her.

Pontos.note: Philo's Demarous fights Pontos in a Hellenized version of West Semitic sea combat.
Philo’s Greek-named Pontos probably continues or interprets the Phoenician divine Sea.

Qodesh-wa-Amrur.note: Athirat’s attendant prepares and accompanies her journey, serving as messenger, driver, or fisherman.
Athirat's divine attendant handles her conveyance during negotiations that secure Baal's palace.

Qos.note: MLKM and QWS occur together in a bilingual inscription, if MLKM denotes Milcom.

Qudshu.note: Resheph and Qudshu appear together in coordinated Egyptian cultic triads.

Qudšu.note: Older scholarship equated Athirat with Qudšu, but the identification is now heavily disputed.

Qudšu-wa-Amrur.note: Athirat's servant transports her to El, indirectly advancing Baal's palace request.

Rahmay.note: Kothar and Rahmay attend the festivities as divine co-guests.

Rahmay.myth: Reconstructed maternity in the birth narrative
Rahmay.note: Rahmay is sometimes reconstructed as the second woman and mother.

Rakabʾel.note: Together they enforce the curse against anyone damaging Kilamuwa’s monument.

Rapiu.note: Rapiu is invoked with or above the underworld Rephaim and may represent their leader.

Raḥmay.note: Athirat and Raḥmay appear together in a nursing formula for the gracious gods.

Re.note: The Egyptian Contendings identifies Anat and Astarte as daughters of Re.
Astarte and Anat are described as daughters of Re in Egyptian theology.
Qadesh bears the Egyptian theological epithet Eye of Re.

Rephan.myth: Tent of Moloch and star of Rephan
Rephan.note: Moloch and Rephan appear together in the Greek Amos tradition.

Reshef-Melqart.note: Successive plaque inscriptions concern work for Reshef-Melqart and later for Tanit.

Ruda.note: Aramaic evidence suggests a protective association or possible identification with Ruda.

Shadrafa.note: Images of both gods may have been offered nearby, without documented joint action.

Shalash.note: Shalash is Dagan's spouse and cultic partner in Syrian and Mesopotamian traditions.

Sid Addir Babi.note: A statue of Horon is apparently vowed to Sid in Sid’s sanctuary.

Smyrna.myth: Smyrna’s incest and the myrrh-tree birth
Smyrna.note: Smyrna becomes a myrrh tree and gives birth to Adonis.

Storm-god.note: The Storm-god reports Ašertu’s conduct, and Elkunirša orders him to humiliate her.
Elkunirša joins Ašertu in plotting against the Storm-god.

Sydyk.note: Sydyk fathers Eshmun, presented as the eighth son and brother of the Cabiri.

Tallay.note: Tallay appears among the female members of Baal's household.

Tanit’s Gad.myth: Worship of Tanit and her Gad
Tanit’s Gad.note: Tanit is worshipped alongside her fortune, tutelary genius, or divine efficacy.

Tarḫunt.note: Hittite-Luwian traditions equated Hadad with their weather-god in multilingual contexts.

Teššub.note: Multilingual scribal and cultic systems translated Hadad through the Hurrian storm-god.
At Ankuwa, Nikkal receives offerings within Teššub's circle rather than Ḫepat's.

The Gracious Gods.myth: Second birth of the voracious gods
The Gracious Gods.note: Probably distinct later offspring of El and the same women.
A disputed interpretation identifies Šaḥar and Šalim with the Gracious Gods.

The Mare.note: Horon neutralizes the serpent poison threatening the Mare or her offspring.

The Mare.myth: Marriage negotiations after the serpent cure
The Mare.note: Horon enters marriage negotiations with her, though no permanent union is established.

The gracious gods.myth: Birth and nursing of the gracious gods
The gracious gods.note: The voracious gracious gods receive milk from Athirat and Raḥmay.

The seventy gods.note: The seventy gods constitute Athirat’s offspring or divine clan, though the synthesis is partly reconstructive.

The stars.note: The birth is followed by a disputed instruction involving Šapšu and the stars.

Theias.myth: Smyrna’s incest and the myrrh-tree birth
Theias.note: Adonis is conceived through Smyrna’s incestuous union with her father Theias.

Thukamuna-and-Shunama.note: Thukamuna-and-Shunama support the intoxicated El and help him home.

Tunnan.note: Anat boasts that she crushed the twisting sea monster Tunnan.
Tunnan may be another name for Lotan, though it may instead be distinct.
Šapšu appears among protective powers against a hostile complex including Tunnan.

Tunnanu.note: The sea-serpent appears in Horon’s magical field, without recoverable direct combat.
Yam is closely associated or possibly identified with Tunnanu; their exact relationship remains disputed.

Tyros.note: Tyros demands a robe matching the purple color produced by Melqart's dog.

Ugar.note: Baal dispatches Ugar as a divine messenger during palace negotiations and communications with Mot.
Ugar carries Baal’s message to Kothar at his distant residence.

Ugaru.note: Baal sends Ugaru as one of his paired messengers to Mot.

Umbu.note: Hurrian sequences placing Umbu before Nikkal most plausibly designate them as a divine couple.

Upper God.note: The Egyptian healing spell calls Nikkal the wife of this foreign god, probably a moon deity.

YHWH.note: YHWH’s captured cult vessels are carried before Chemosh after Nebo’s destruction.
Chemosh and YHWH are rhetorically juxtaposed as rival grantors of territory.
Dagon's image falls before YHWH's Ark and is found beheaded and dismembered.

YHWH.myth: Prohibition and judgment of Molech worship
YHWH.note: YHWH prohibits offerings to Molech and threatens offenders with expulsion.

YHWH.myth: Repudiation of the Jerusalem Molech rite
YHWH.note: YHWH condemns passing children to Molech and denies commanding it.
YHWH destroys Rephaite-related populations and transfers their territories to Moab, Ammon, and Israel.
The dead Rephaim cannot rise or praise YHWH, emphasizing their impotence.
YHWH divides personified Sea while crushing dragons and Leviathan.
YHWH controls the raging Sea as an expression of incomparable kingship.
Divine power stills personified Sea and strikes Rahab.

YHWH.myth: YHWH marches against Sea and Rivers
YHWH.note: YHWH advances against Sea and Rivers in storm-warrior imagery.
YHWH dries Sea, transforming primordial combat imagery into Exodus deliverance.

Yabdaray.note: Yabdaray is apparently offered to Yarikh instead of Nikkal, but Yarikh refuses her.

Yahu.note: Anat-Yahu may denote consortship, hypostasis, or a compound divine title.

Yahweh.note: Regional blessings associate Yahweh with his ʾšrth, possibly a consort, manifestation, or cult symbol.
Their worshippers contest which deity answers by fire and controls rain; the gods never meet directly.
Hebrew texts identify Yahweh with El’s titles, attributes, and patriarchal identity.
One disputed reading makes El or Elyon allot Israel to Yahweh.
Yahweh assumes the dragon-slayer role against Leviathan, Lotan’s later Hebrew heir.

Yahweh.myth: Yahweh condemns Solomon’s worship of Milcom
Yahweh.note: Yahweh condemns Milcom’s worship and announces the division of Solomon’s kingdom.
Resheph marches at Yahweh’s feet as a subordinated pestilential attendant.

Yamm.note: Athirat may participate in deliberations about Yamm’s kingship; her sea-related title remains disputed.
El favors Yamm’s kingship and calls him Beloved of El.
El authorizes construction of a dwelling for Yamm.
Šapšu reports or mediates El’s appointment of Yamm; no combat occurs.

Yammu.note: Baal strikes Yammu with Kothar's clubs, defeats him, and secures kingship.

Zabib.note: Anat includes the female enemy Zabib in her catalogue of victories.

Zamzummim.note: The Ammonite name Zamzummim designates inhabitants regarded as Rephaim.

Zeus Arotrios.myth: Dagon discovers grain and the plough
Zeus Arotrios.note: Philo identifies the agricultural culture-bringer Dagon with Ploughman Zeus.

Zeus Demarous.note: Astarte and Zeus Demarous rule jointly with Adodos under Kronos.

Zeus Meilichios.note: Philo reports that Chousor was honored or interpreted as Zeus Meilichios.

boar.note: A wounded boar gores Adonis in the groin and kills him.

serpent/venom deities.note: Localized Astartes participate with divine powers in ritual sequences countering snake venom.

the holy gods of Byblos.note: Baalat Gebal and Byblos’s divine assembly are invoked to preserve Yehimilk.

the sons of El.note: El is the corporate father and patriarch of the divine assembly.

Šagar.note: A damaged passage pairs Šagar with an Ashtar or Ishtar form without narrative action.

Šamaš.note: Multilingual god lists equate Šapšu with the normally male Akkadian solar god Šamaš.

Šapšu.note: An offering or presentation before Šapšu and the stars follows their birth.
Šapšu carries an appeal to the pair in heaven against serpent venom.

Šassūrātu.note: A multilingual god list treats Šassūrātu as the Kotharat’s Akkadian counterpart.

Šauška.note: Nikkal receives offerings in a mixed ritual centered on Šauška and Ashtart.

Šaʿtiqatu.note: El creates the female healing being when the assembled gods cannot cure Kirta.

ʿAshtar.note: The compound ʿAshtar-Chemosh receives Nebo under the sacred ban.

ʿAthtapar.note: ʿAthtapar and the pair occur in the same divine sequence.

ʿAthtart.note: ʿAthtart and the pair are co-invoked against poison.

Ḏāt Ḥimyam.note: Athtar appears with Ḏāt Ḥimyam in invocations protecting dedicants, families, and property.

Ḥirta.note: Resheph and Ḥirta appear together with Nanaya in Palmyrene dedications.

Ḫarḫab.note: Nikkal’s father is named in the wedding composition invoking the Kotharat.

Ḫepat.note: Nikkal belongs to Ḫepat's ordered offering circle without an asserted blood relationship.

Ḫiriḫibi.note: He negotiates Yarikh’s marriage in the composition that invokes the Kotharat.

Ḫirḫib.myth: The Wedding of Nikkal and Yarikh
Ḫirḫib.note: Nikkal is his daughter; he negotiates her marriage and proposes alternative brides to Yarikh.

Ḫirḫibi.note: Yarikh negotiates with Nikkal’s father, who initially proposes another bride.

Ḫutena and Ḫutellura.note: Multilingual god-list tradition treats the Hurrian birth and fate goddesses as counterparts.

Ṭallay.note: Ṭallay is named as one of Baal's three daughters.

Ẓiẓẓu.note: Ẓiẓẓu and the pair are co-invoked without a narrated interaction.

Ẓiẓẓu-wa-Kāmaṯu.note: These obscure paired figures occur within the invocation series headed by Horon.
